name: Saw palmetto extract

card.summary: A plant extract from Serenoa repens berries, taken orally or applied to the scalp by people who want to reduce DHT activity and slow male-pattern hair thinning.
card.aka: Serenoa repens, saw palmetto berry extract, Permixon (a standardized product)
card.note: May interact with anticoagulants and lower PSA readings; avoided in pregnancy.

quick.overview:
Saw palmetto extract comes from the berries of a small palm native to the southeastern United States. It is sold as a supplement, mainly for urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate, and is also used by people with male-pattern hair loss who want a plant-based option.

The appearance payoff is hair retention: the extract is reported to inhibit 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that makes DHT, the hormone linked to follicle miniaturization. Small hair studies have reported improvements, and a 2026 network meta-analysis listed saw palmetto among effective off-label options, though authors call for better comparative trials.
quick.how: People take it as an oral capsule or use shampoos and topical products that contain it, often alongside other hair-care measures. Users describe waiting several months to judge changes, as with other hair-loss approaches.
quick.risks: Side effects are generally mild, such as stomach upset, headache or dizziness. It may add to bleeding risk with anticoagulants, can lower PSA test results, and is not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

lead: Saw palmetto extract is made from the ripe berries of Serenoa repens, a low palm of the southeastern United States, and is sold as a dietary supplement [1][2]. Its main established market use is for lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia, but it has also become a popular supplement among people with androgenetic alopecia.

For hair, the appeal is mechanistic: the extract is reported to inhibit 5-alpha-reductase, reducing conversion of testosterone to DHT, the hormone implicated in miniaturization of scalp follicles [1][4]. People use it by mouth or in topical products as a milder alternative or addition to approved treatments.

Research exists but is mixed: topical and oral hair studies are mostly small and often combine saw palmetto with other agents [3]. Prostate trials are inconsistent, including a large industry-independent trial that did not find a benefit [5].

chain: Lower DHT activity at the follicle
Slower thinning and more retained hair
angle.text: Users take it hoping to slow DHT-driven thinning at the hairline and crown. Some use it as an add-on to other treatments and others as a plant-based alternative.

infobox: Serenoa repens, native to the southeastern US and Caribbean [2][12]
Dietary supplement; not FDA-approved before sale [12]

paras: People with male-pattern hair loss use saw palmetto orally or in topical products to slow thinning [3]. A 2025 review of topical hair products listed saw palmetto among popular actives, noting that most studies combine it with other agents and have small samples or conflicts of interest [3].

It is mainly used for urinary symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia. Reviews describe inconsistent results, partly due to non-standardized extracts, with hexane-based extracts giving more consistent outcomes [4].

Saw palmetto is promoted for urinary symptoms of an enlarged prostate, male pattern baldness and chronic prostatitis or pelvic pain, according to the NIH's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.[12] The extract is made from the dark berries, which contain phytosterols, free fatty acids, flavonoids and polysaccharides, and Wikipedia notes its use in folk medicine for coughs and other complaints.[2]

The extract contains fatty acids and phytosterols; laboratory work suggests inhibition of 5-alpha-reductase and anti-inflammatory activity [4][10]. A 2025 laboratory study reported 5-alpha-reductase regulation and apoptosis effects in vitro and in animals [10].

A 2009 commentary in the Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery described Serenoa repens as a natural 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor widely sold directly to consumers for androgenetic alopecia, called for larger trials, and cautioned that self-treatment could delay detection of prostate problems.[11]

In a two-year open-label comparison of 100 men with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia, hair growth judged from global photographs improved in 38 percent of men taking saw palmetto and 68 percent of men taking finasteride; the authors concluded saw palmetto may improve androgenetic alopecia but that finasteride was more effective.[11]

A pilot open-label study of 50 men aged 20 to 50 using topical Serenoa repens products for 24 weeks reported higher average and terminal hair counts at weeks 12 and 24 than at baseline, with some gains levelling off by week 24 and limited side effects; the study had no placebo group.[11]

A 2025 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a bioactive fatty-acid saw palmetto extract enrolled 60 adults with self-perceived thinning hair, about half women. Its 90-day interim results reported increases in terminal and total hair counts and reduced shedding versus placebo, with no adverse events.[11]
NCCIH states that a few small studies have tested oral and topical use for hair loss and that the evidence is too limited for conclusions.[12]

Mild digestive upset, headache and dizziness are the most common reports.[12] NCCIH reports it has been used in research for up to three years and may be unsafe in pregnancy or breastfeeding; Wikipedia adds that it is not recommended for children under 12 because of possible effects on androgen and estrogen metabolism.[2][12] Sources differ on PSA: Wikipedia, citing a 2009 commentary, says it can lower PSA and mask prostate cancer signals, while NCCIH says it does not appear to affect PSA readings.[2][12] Wikipedia also notes a possible additive bleeding effect with anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs.[2]

A 2025 systematic review and network meta-analysis compared dietary supplements for androgenetic alopecia using hair density outcomes and noted limits such as small samples and few direct comparisons [6]. A 2026 network meta-analysis of off-label therapies for male androgenetic alopecia ranked saw palmetto among the effective off-label options while calling for higher-quality comparative trials [9].
For urinary symptoms, a New England Journal of Medicine trial in 2006 found no effect of the studied extract against placebo [5], whereas other trials and reviews report symptom improvements [7][8].

A 2023 review of 27 studies found saw palmetto alone provides little or no benefit for urinary symptoms of BPH, and a 2022 review found no significant benefit for chronic prostatitis, according to NCCIH.[12]

timeline.event: A New England Journal of Medicine randomized trial tests saw palmetto extract against placebo for prostate symptoms [5].
A commentary notes saw palmetto is widely sold for androgenetic alopecia and calls for larger trials.[11]
A two-year open-label study compares saw palmetto with finasteride in 100 men.[11]
A pilot study of topical Serenoa repens in 50 men is published.[11]
A network meta-analysis compares dietary supplements for androgenetic alopecia [6].
